claims.text: The starting eutectic high-entropy alloy has a dual-phase lamellar microstructure.
The lamellae are organized into a hierarchical colony structure.
Strong internal interfaces in the untreated alloy cause dislocation pile-ups during room-temperature tension.
Dislocation pile-ups at internal boundaries generate local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic failure.
A controlled thermal or thermomechanical treatment can form thin, continuous nanoscale interphase complexion layers along the lamellar boundaries.
The treatment-induced interphase layers will be ductile.
The ductile interphase layers will act as dislocation sinks that absorb or deflect dislocations.
Enabling plastic accommodation at lamellar interfaces can alleviate local stress concentrations rather than produce cracks.
Reducing pile-ups and local stress concentrations will delay crack nucleation and propagation.
The treatment will increase room-temperature tensile ductility relative to the untreated alloy.
The treatment will maintain or slightly increase tensile strength relative to the untreated alloy.
The desired response depends on producing a continuous nanoscale interphase without overaging or coarsening the lamellar structure.
Treated and untreated samples should be compared by room-temperature uniaxial tensile testing under the same mechanical conditions.
TEM can be used to verify interphase-layer formation, continuity, and thickness at the lamellar boundaries.
The hypothesis is operationally falsified if no continuous nanoscale interphase forms, or if ductility does not improve significantly without a loss of tensile strength.
